messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
I want to try a three-motor cluster, nothing above a C. It should get to roughly 1,000 ft. Keep the landing under 5.5 m/s. Our pad has a 3 ft rod. What would you build?

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 1,000 ft = 1000 * 0.3048 = 305 m (approximate, aim within 5%). Three motors in one cluster, each at most C class (fixed). Touchdown under 5.5 m/s (maximum). Rail is only 3 ft = 3 * 0.3048 = 0.91 m (fixed; the binding constraint — a short rod demands high thrust). Wind not stated, assume 2 m/s. Single stage.
2. Feasibility: clearing 15 m/s off a 0.91 m rod needs a >= 15^2 / (2 * 0.91) = 124 m/s^2 of acceleration. Three C6s only make about 14.4 N total, which caps liftoff near 0.108 kg — lighter than any triple-mount airframe I can build. The cluster needs higher-thrust C motors. Checking C6, C11, C12 and B6 for thrust, mass and diameter.

2. Feasibility: the Quest C12 is the answer — 11.9 N average each, so three of them give 3 * 11.9 = 35.7 N on only 3 * 0.0237 = 0.071 kg of motors, and they are still C class at 9.9 N*s apiece. The C11 offers similar thrust but is 24 mm wide and heavier; the C6 and B6 cannot lift a cluster off a 0.91 m rod. Maximum liftoff mass for rail exit is about 35.7 / (124 + 9.81) = 0.267 kg.
3. Size: airframe about 0.10 kg plus motors gives liftoff near 0.175 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 35.7 / (0.175 * 9.81) = 20.8. On the rod a = (35.7 - 1.72) / 0.175 = 194 m/s^2, so v = sqrt(2 * 194 * 0.91) = 18.8 m/s at exit. Ideal delta-v = 29.7 / 0.175 = 170 m/s; a 45 mm airframe burns a lot of that to drag, so the result should land in the few-hundred-metre band around the goal. Three 19.5 mm mounts pack a cluster span of 19.5 * 2.155 = 42.0 mm, which needs a body ID of at least 42 mm — a 45 mm tube with 0.8 mm walls leaves 43.4 mm. Descent mass about 0.175 - 0.0312 = 0.14 kg; a 0.40 m chute at Cd 0.8 gives sqrt(2 * 0.14 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 0.126)) = 4.7 m/s. Delay: three ejection charges fire together, so ignition redundancy is built in; C12 offers 4, 6 and 8 s, and for a ~300 m flight I'll take the 4 s option.
4. Draft: 45 mm card body, 0.50 m long, hollow plastic ogive nose, four balsa fins, triple 19.5 mm mounts on two plywood rings, Quest C12-4s, 0.40 m chute. Simulating on the 0.91 m rod.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulated apogee of 367.8 m is 21% over the 305 m goal, outside the 5% band. Stability at rail exit is 0.86 cal against the 1.0 cal gate, a real failure. And the chute fired at 4.9 s while apogee was at 5.46 s, so it opened at 25.6 m/s and drew a high-speed deployment warning. Good numbers: rail exit 19.4 m/s off the short rod, thrust-to-weight 24.9, touchdown 4.6 m/s. Liftoff mass came back 0.146 kg, lighter than my 0.175 kg guess.
5. Fix: three items, two changes. Margin 0.86 cal vs the 1.0 gate and the 21% altitude overshoot share one cause — not enough fin area aft — so fins grow: root 0.08 to 0.10 m, span 0.05 to 0.065 m, tip 0.04 to 0.05 m, about 60% more area, moving CP aft and adding drag. Separately, the 25.6 m/s deployment comes from the 4 s delay firing 0.5 s before apogee; the C12's 6 s option puts ejection about 1.5 s past apogee on this trajectory. Re-simulating.
